questions.stem: A discrete random variable \(X\) has the probability distribution shown below, where \(m\) is a constant.

figure.svg: fig:cb189500c7

parts.stem: (a) Find the value of \(m\).
parts.hint: All probabilities in a distribution must sum to 1.

steps.explain: The sum of all probabilities in the table must equal 1.

figure.svg: fig:cb189500c7

steps.explain: Solve for \(m\).

parts.stem: (b) Using \(m=0.16\), calculate the expected value \(E(X)\).
parts.hint: Use \(E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(x)\).

steps.explain: Multiply each \(x\)-value by its probability and add the results.

figure.svg: fig:a610e7cd2f

steps.explain: Evaluate each term and sum.

parts.stem: (c) Calculate the variance \(\text{Var}(X)\), correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.hint: Use \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\).

steps.explain: Calculate \(E(X^2)\) by multiplying each \(x^2\)-value by its probability and summing.
Subtract \([E(X)]^2\) using the value \(E(X)=21.72\) found in part (b).
Complete the subtraction.

questions.stem:
A discrete probability distribution is shown below.

$$ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} X=x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.23 & 0.38 & 0.21 & 0.13 & 0.05 \end{array} $$

What is the expected value \( E(X) \)?

steps.explain: The expected value of a discrete random variable is \( E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(X=x) \) — multiply each outcome by its probability and add the results.
Substitute every \( (x, P(X=x)) \) pair from the table.
Evaluate each product.
Add the products to get the final expected value.

questions.stem: The discrete random variable \(X\) has the probability distribution shown below.

parts.stem: (a) Find \(P(1 < X \le 3)\).
parts.hint: \(1 < X \le 3\) means \(X=2\) or \(X=3\) — it does NOT include \(X=1\), since the inequality is strict there.

steps.explain: The condition \(1 < X \le 3\) includes \(X=2\) and \(X=3\), but excludes \(X=1\) (since the inequality on that side is strict).
Substitute the given probabilities and add.

parts.stem: (b) Find the variance of \(X\).
parts.hint: First find \(\mu = E(X)\), then use \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2\).

steps.explain: Find the mean \(\mu=E(X)\) by multiplying each \(x\)-value by its probability and summing.
Find \(E(X^2)\) by multiplying each \(x^2\)-value by its probability and summing.
Use the variance formula \(\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2\).

questions.stem: A teacher asked fifty students to identify their favourite type of pet. A partially completed Pareto chart shows some of the data collected. How many students picked cats as their favourite pet?

figure.svg: fig:d1ba111e96

steps.explain: In a Pareto chart, each category's own frequency is the GAP between its cumulative percentage and the previous category's cumulative percentage. From the chart, Dogs reach \(40\%\) cumulative, and Cats reach \(68\%\) cumulative.

figure.svg: fig:e2fa9579f3

steps.explain: All probabilities must sum to 1. Add all five probabilities in terms of \(r\) and solve.
Find \(E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(X{=}x)\), using the now-known probabilities \(\frac{1}{9},\frac{2}{9},\frac{3}{9},\frac{2}{9},\frac{1}{9}\).
Find \(E(X^2) = \sum x^2 \cdot P(X{=}x)\).
Apply the variance formula \(Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\).

A Year 11 class conducted a survey on the number of books students read during a school year. The data was collected and grouped as follows:

Class Interval (x)Class centreFrequencyCumulative frequency
0–4233
5–97710
10–1412A24
15–19171034
20–2422640

parts.stem: Find the value of A.
parts.hint: The cumulative frequency for 10-14 is the sum of all frequencies up to and including that class.

steps.explain: The probabilities must add to \(1\). Using the rows in the question gives \(4a+3b=1\). With \(b=2a\), solve for \(a\) and \(b\).
Now calculate the mean and the second moment from \(x=0,1,2,3,4\).
Variance equals the second moment minus the square of the mean.

parts.stem: Let \(p=\frac23\). Find \(E(X)\), correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.hint: Substitute \(p=\dfrac23\) into the probabilities for \(x=1\) and \(x=3\), then use \(E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)\).

steps.explain: The values are \(x=0,1,2,3\). With \(p=\dfrac23\), the probabilities are \(0.1\), \(0.6\left(\dfrac23\right)^2\), \(0.3\) and \(1-\dfrac23\).
Multiply each \(x\)-value by its probability and add. The \(x=0\) term contributes zero.
Round to two decimal places.

Divide both sides by 0.30.

steps.explain: The cumulative frequency \(X\) for the \(10-19\) class is the total count of students in the \(0-9\) AND \(10-19\) classes combined, after the 2 absent students' data is added somewhere in the table.

Before adding the 2 new students, this total is \(4+5=9\). The 2 new students could each land in the \(0-9\) class, the \(10-19\) class, a HIGHER class, or a mix — so \(X\) can only increase by 0, 1, or 2 from this base of 9, depending on where they fall.
Comparing this possible range to the given options, only \(X=10\) falls inside \(\{9,10,11\}\) — the others (12, 14, 16) are all too large to be possible.

The range is the difference between the maximum and minimum observed values: \(6 - 1 = 5\). This is also true.
Therefore, the only false statement is \"The mode is 6\".

questions.stem: A set of data has a lower quartile of 22 and an upper quartile of 32. What is the maximum possible range for this set of data if there are no outliers?
questions.hint: A value is an OUTLIER if it is more than \(1.5\times\text{IQR}\) below \(Q_1\) or above \(Q_3\). The biggest possible range uses the two most extreme values that are still NOT outliers.

steps.explain: Interquartile range.
Lower fence (smallest value that is not an outlier).
Upper fence (largest value that is not an outlier).
Maximum range = largest allowed value − smallest allowed value.

keyPoints.note: Use the outlier fences: Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR.
Data must lie between the two fences.

steps.explain: Follow the dashed line across to the RIGHT axis and read the percentage.
Check with the counts: the bars total about \(1100+500+100+90+60+35+25+5\approx1915\), and \(\dfrac{1100}{1915}\approx57\%\) ✓.
Why not 1100? That is the NUMBER of complaints, not the percentage.

keyPoints.note: Read the first cumulative point on the right-hand axis.

meta.source: Hurlstone Agricultural High School 2020 Mathematics Advanced Trial HSC

questions.stem: The Pareto chart shows complaints about the delivery of pizzas from a new pizza store. Use the graph to answer: Explain how the Pareto principle can be used by the pizza company to direct their efforts to improve the customer experience.

options: Focus first on 'Delivery delayed' and 'Pizza not hot': these two causes (a quarter of the categories) account for about 80% of complaints
Spread effort equally over all eight causes, because each cause matters equally
Fix 'Not baked properly' first, because it is the smallest cause
Ignore the tallest bars, because they are too hard to fix
questions.hint: The PARETO PRINCIPLE says about 80% of the effects come from about 20% of the causes. Use the cumulative line to see which few categories account for most complaints, and fix those first.

steps.explain: Read the cumulative line after each bar: first bar about 57%, after the first TWO bars about 83%.

questions.stem: The graph shows a scatterplot for a set of data. Which of the following values is the most appropriate Pearson's correlation coefficient for this data?
questions.hint: The points trend downward but do not sit tightly on a straight line — a value between 0 and \(-1\), moderately strong, is appropriate.

steps.explain: As \(x\) increases, \(y\) tends to decrease — the trend is negative, ruling out any positive value.
The points show a fairly consistent downward pattern but with some scatter — not perfectly linear (which would be exactly \(-1\)), but stronger than a weak correlation like \(-0.35\).
The value that best matches "negative, moderately strong" is \(-0.63\).

questions.stem:
The table below shows data for 10 countries: research spending (% of GDP) \(x\) and cases of Figtree Syndrome (1000s) \(y\).

| \(x\) | 2.0 | 2.4 | 3.0 | 3.2 | 3.5 | 3.8 | 4.1 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 5.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 7.8 | 6.8 | 7.2 | 6.6 | 5.8 | 5.6 | 4.6 | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.2 |

Determine Pearson's correlation coefficient for this data correct to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Use a calculator with statistical functions. Enter the data as bivariate pairs and compute the correlation coefficient.
questions.solution: Using a calculator: \(r \approx -0.949\). The strong negative correlation indicates that as research spending increases, cases of Figtree Syndrome decrease.

steps.explain:
To find Pearson's correlation coefficient (\(r\)) using a Casio fx-82AU PLUS calculator, first set it to the correct statistical mode for bivariate (two-variable) data.

1. Press **MODE**, then select **2 (STAT)**.
2. Select **2 (A+BX)** for linear regression.

Next, input your data into the table that appears on the screen.

1. Enter all the \(x\)-values in the left column, pressing **=** after each number.
2. Use the arrow keys to move to the top of the \(y\)-column.
3. Enter the corresponding \(y\)-values, pressing **=** after each one.
4. Once all data is entered, press **AC**. (Don't worry, your data is saved in the calculator's memory!)

Finally, retrieve the correlation coefficient \(r\) from the regression menu.

1. Press **SHIFT** and then **1 (STAT)**.
2. Select **5 (Reg)** for regression variables.
3. Select **3 (r)** for Pearson's correlation coefficient.
4. Press **=** to calculate the value.

Rounding to 3 decimal places, you should get \(-0.949\).

questions.hint: Look at the DIRECTION of the points (up or down as you move right) and how tightly they cluster round a straight line.

steps.explain: Direction: as the dosage increases (moving right), the reported pain generally DECREASES (moving down) → NEGATIVE correlation.
Strength: the points follow a downward trend but with noticeable scatter (they do not lie close to the red line) → MODERATE.
Combine direction and strength.
Why not 'no correlation'? The points clearly trend downwards.

keyPoints.note: Direction of the trend, then how tight the points are.

Answer correct to 4 decimal places.

questions.stem:
Figtree Syndrome is a rare disease. The table shows research spending (% of GDP) $x$ and cases of Figtree Syndrome (1000s) $y$ for 10 countries.

| $x$ | 2.0 | 2.4 | 3.0 | 3.2 | 3.5 | 3.8 | 4.1 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 5.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 7.8 | 6.8 | 7.2 | 6.6 | 5.8 | 5.6 | 4.6 | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.2 |

parts.stem: Find the least squares regression line for this data. Round your values to 3 significant figures.

steps.explain: Assuming you still have the data entered from Q17(a) in your Casio fx-82AU PLUS calculator. (If not, press **MODE** $\rightarrow$ **2 (STAT)** $\rightarrow$ **2 (A+BX)**, enter the $x$ and $y$ values, and press **AC**).

To find the $y$-intercept ($a$) of the least squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$:

1. Press **SHIFT** and then **1 (STAT)**.
2. Select **5 (Reg)**.
3. Select **1 (A)**.
4. Press **=** to calculate.

Rounding to 3 significant figures, $a \approx 10.4$.

To find the slope ($b$) of the regression line:

1. Press **SHIFT** and then **1 (STAT)**.
2. Select **5 (Reg)**.
3. Select **2 (B)**.
4. Press **=** to calculate.

Rounding to 3 significant figures, $b \approx -1.28$.
Construct the final regression equation by substituting your calculated $a$ and $b$ into the formula $\hat{y} = a + bx$.

questions.hint: Use your calculator's linear regression function to find the slope $b$ and intercept $a$ of $\hat{y} = a + bx$.
questions.solution: Using the calculator: slope $b \approx -1.28$, intercept $a \approx 10.4$. Regression line: $\hat{y} = -1.28x + 10.4$.

questions.stem: Max surveyed a group of people about their age and weekly wage. \\ \(\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{Age (years)}\ x & 18 & 45 & 28 & 15 & 32 & 68 \\ \hline \text{Wage (\$/week)}\ W & 715 & 2350 & 1530 & 438 & 1690 & 1320 \end{array}\)

parts.stem: (a) Find the correlation coefficient \( r \), and classify the type and strength of correlation.

steps.explain: Using a Casio fx-82AU PLUS II calculator, first set it to Statistical Linear Regression mode by pressing **[MODE] → [2] (STAT) → [2] (A+BX)**.
Enter the data into the X (Age) and Y (Wage) columns, pressing **[=]** after each value. Once all 6 pairs are entered, press **[AC]** to clear the screen (the data is safely saved).
To find the correlation coefficient \( r \), press **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [3] (r) → [=]**.
Since \( r \approx 0.53 \) is between 0.5 and 0.7, it represents a moderate positive correlation (wage tends to increase moderately with age).

parts.stem: (b) Find the equation of the least-squares regression line in the form \( W=Bx+A \), where \( A \) and \( B \) are integers.

steps.explain: Continuing with the saved data on your calculator, you can find the regression coefficients \( A \) (y-intercept) and \( B \) (gradient).
Find the y-intercept \( A \) by pressing **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [1] (A) → [=]**.
Find the gradient \( B \) by pressing **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [2] (B) → [=]**.
Round both values to the nearest integer as required (A = 706, B = 18) and substitute them into the regression equation \( W = Bx + A \).

parts.stem: (c) Use the equation from part (b) to estimate the earnings of a 50-year-old worker.

steps.explain: Substitute \( x=50 \) into the regression equation \( W=18x+706 \) found in part (b).
Evaluate the multiplication, then add.
State the estimated weekly wage.

parts.stem: (d) Could your equation from part (b) be used to make valid estimates for ages greater than 68 and less than 15 years? Validate your response with calculations and/or reasons.
parts.answer: No — extrapolating beyond the sample's age range (15 to 68 years) is unreliable, since there is no data confirming the linear trend continues outside that range.

steps.explain: The regression line was fitted using only the six data points, whose ages range from the youngest (15) to the oldest (68) in the sample.

Using the equation to predict outcomes for \( x \)-values outside this range is called extrapolation. There is no evidence that the same linear trend continues beyond the range that was actually observed — the relationship could level off, reverse, or become non-linear (e.g. wages typically don't keep rising indefinitely with age, especially near or after retirement).

Note that a moderate correlation coefficient (from part (a)) describes the strength of the relationship WITHIN the observed data — it says nothing about whether that relationship still holds outside the sampled range.

Part (a): using the six data pairs (age, wage) — (18,715), (45,2350), (28,1530), (15,438), (32,1690), (68,1320) — compute the correlation coefficient r using the standard formula (or calculator statistics mode).
steps.work: \(r = \dfrac{n\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{\sqrt{\left[n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2\right]\left[n\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2\right]}}\)\\ Evaluating with the six data points gives \(r \approx 0.87\).

steps.explain: Interpret the value of r.
steps.work: Since \(r \approx 0.87\) is close to 1 and positive, this indicates a strong, positive linear correlation between age and wage.

steps.explain: Part (b): find the least-squares regression line \(W = Bx + A\) using the standard formulas \(B=\dfrac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}\) and \(A=\bar{y}-B\bar{x}\) (or calculator regression mode).
steps.work: Using the six data points: \(B \approx 31.5\), \(A \approx -15.4\)\\ So the regression line is \(W \approx 31.5x - 15.4\)

steps.explain: Part (c): substitute \(x=50\) into the regression equation to estimate the wage of a 50-year-old.
Part (d): assess whether the regression equation can be validly used outside the range of the original data (ages 15 to 68).
steps.work: No. Using the equation for ages below 15 or above 68 requires extrapolation beyond the range of the collected data. The linear trend observed within \([15,68]\) is not guaranteed to continue outside this range (e.g. wages typically decline near/after retirement age, and there is no data to confirm the relationship holds for children), so predictions outside this range are not reliable.

parts.stem: (a) Find the least-squares regression line \( y=A+Bx \), and use it to estimate the withdrawal amount (to the nearest $10) when the time until the next withdrawal is 120 hours.

steps.explain: Press \(\text{MODE}\), then select \(\text{STAT}\) (option 2), then select \(\text{2: A+BX}\) for linear regression. A two-column table (X, Y) appears.
Type each X-value then press \(=\) to move to the Y column, type the matching Y-value, then press \(=\) again to move to the next row. Repeat for all 10 withdrawal pairs from the table.

Once all 10 pairs are entered, press \(\text{AC}\) to leave the table (the data stays stored). Then press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) to open the STAT menu, select \(\text{5: Reg}\), then \(\text{1: A}\) to read off the intercept.
Press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) again, select \(\text{5: Reg}\), then \(\text{2: B}\) to read off the gradient. Together, \(A\) and \(B\) give the regression equation \(y=A+Bx\).
Substitute \(y=120\) into the regression equation and solve for \(x\) (withdrawal amount).
Round the estimate to the nearest $10. Since $52.79 is closer to $50 than to $60, the nearest-$10 estimate is $50.

parts.stem: (b) Find the correlation coefficient \( r \) and describe the nature of the relationship.

steps.explain: The data is already stored in two-variable statistics mode from part (a) — no need to re-enter it. Press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) to open the STAT menu, then select \(\text{5: Reg}\).
From the Reg submenu, select \(\text{3: r}\) to read off the correlation coefficient directly.
Since \(r\) is positive, larger withdrawal amounts are associated with longer waits until the next withdrawal.

Since \(|r|\) is close to \(1\) (well above \(0.7\)), classify the strength. Pitfall: reading the sign of \(r\) incorrectly off the calculator display gives the negative-correlation distractor — double-check the displayed sign before rounding.

The number of weeks they have been working (\(x\)) and the number of times they ask for assistance during a four-hour shift (\(y\)) are: \((2,15), (6,10), (10,6), (17,3)\). Use a calculator to find the equation of the least-squares regression line for this dataset, finding the gradient and \(y\)-intercept to 2 decimal places.

steps.explain: On your calculator, enter the four data points into two-variable (bivariate) statistics mode, then request the linear regression coefficients.
Reading the gradient (\(b\)) and \(y\)-intercept (\(a\)) from the calculator's regression output, rounded to 2 decimal places.
Write the full equation of the regression line.

meta.source: Hills Grammar 2025 2U Trials

questions.stem: Using the least-squares regression line \(y=-0.79x+15.38\) as a guide, on average how many full weeks will an employee have been working before they require assistance less than 8 times during a four-hour shift?

steps.explain: Find the value of \(x\) where the regression line predicts exactly \(y=8\), by substituting and solving.
Rearrange to solve for \(x\).

Since the gradient is negative (\(y\) decreases as \(x\) increases), assistance requests drop below 8 only once \(x\) exceeds \(9.34\) weeks. Check the next WHOLE (full) week: at \(x=9\), \(y\approx 15.38-0.79(9)=8.27>8\) still, but at \(x=10\), \(y\approx 15.38-0.79(10)=7.48<8\).
The first full week where the prediction drops below 8 is week 10.

meta.source: Hills Grammar 2025 2U Trials

questions.hint: Use linear regression on the calculator: \(h=mt+c\) with \(m\) the gradient and \(c\) the intercept. The trees grow taller with time, so \(m>0\).

steps.explain: Enter the 8 recorded pairs into linear regression.
Read the gradient.
Read the intercept.
Write the line (2 decimal places).

keyPoints.note: Use linear regression on the calculator with the 8 recorded pairs.

questions.stem: Hayden is an agricultural scientist studying the growth of a particular tree over several years. The data he recorded is shown in the table below (the height after 5 years was not recorded). A scatterplot of the data is also shown. Hayden did not record the tree’s height after five years. Using the line \(h=1.19t-0.85\), predict the height after five years, correct to one decimal place.

questions.stem: Hayden is an agricultural scientist studying the growth of a particular tree over several years. The data he recorded is shown in the table below (the height after 5 years was not recorded). A scatterplot of the data is also shown. Using the line \(h=1.19t-0.85\), use algebra to estimate how many years it will take for the tree to reach a height of 20 metres. Answer correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.explain: Substitute \(h=20\).
Add 0.85 to both sides.
Divide by 1.19.
Why not 16.8? \(20\div1.19=16.8\) ignores the intercept \(-0.85\). Why not 23.8? That multiplies \(20\times1.19\) instead of solving the equation.

Neither is reliable because one data point is missing

steps.explain: The least-squares line minimises the squares of the vertical distances from the points to the line. The sums needed are \(\sum t=40\), \(\sum h=40.7\), \(\sum t^{2}=260\), \(\sum th=274.7\).
Gradient: \(b=\dfrac{n\sum th-\sum t\sum h}{n\sum t^{2}-\left(\sum t\right)^{2}}\).
Intercept: \(a=\bar h-b\bar t\) with \(\bar t=\dfrac{40}{8}=5\) and \(\bar h=\dfrac{40.7}{8}\approx 5.0875\).
Write the line in the form \(h=a+bt\) (red line through the data).

steps.explain: Check the sign: the points rise as \(t\) increases, so the gradient must be POSITIVE (this rules out option C). The line passes just below the origin (when \(t=0\), \(h\approx-0.85\)), so the intercept is negative (rules out D) and the gradient, not the intercept, is 1.19 (rules out B).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the equation of the least-squares line of best fit
keyPoints.note: Use the calculator regression on the recorded data only; gradient is the coefficient of t.

meta.source: Killara High School 2020 Year 12 Trial Examination Mathematics Advanced

questions.stem: Hayden is studying the growth of a tree. The least-squares line of best fit is \(h=-0.85+1.19t\) (\(t\) = years since planting, \(h\) = height in metres). Hayden did not record the tree's height after five years. Predict the height after five years, correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Substitute \(t=5\) into the equation of the line of best fit.

steps.explain: We need the height when \(t=5\), so substitute 5 for \(t\) in \(h=-0.85+1.19t\) (orange point on the line).

Add.

So the correct choice is option A.

A prediction OUTSIDE the range (e.g. year 20) would be extrapolation and is much less reliable because the pattern may not continue.
Option D is false: the points are close to the line but not on it. Option C is false: reliability depends on interpolation versus extrapolation and how linear the data are.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Inside the data range = interpolation (reliable); outside = extrapolation (unreliable).

questions.stem: Using the equation \(h=-0.85+1.19t\) (\(t\) = years since planting, \(h\) = height in metres) that was determined for Hayden's tree data, interpret the slope of the least-squares regression line in terms of the variables height and years. Which interpretation is correct?
options: On average, the tree grows about 1.19 metres taller each year.
The tree was 1.19 metres tall when it was planted.
On average, the tree grows 0.85 metres each year.
The tree gets 1.19 years older each metre it grows.
questions.hint: The slope is the change in \(h\) for each 1-unit increase in \(t\). Put the units in: metres per year.

steps.explain: In \(h=-0.85+1.19t\) the slope (gradient) is the number multiplying \(t\), which is 1.19.
Slope \(=\dfrac{\text{change in }h}{\text{change in }t}\): when \(t\) increases by 1 year, \(h\) increases by 1.19 metres.
So the average growth rate of the tree is 1.19 metres per year.

Option B describes the INTERCEPT (value of \(h\) at \(t=0\)); and the intercept here is \(-0.85\), which is not a sensible height, only a fitted value. Option C uses the intercept as the slope. Option D swaps the variables.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Slope = change in the y-variable per 1 unit of the x-variable; state it with units.

questions.hint: The two tests are out of different totals, so change Test 2 to a mark out of 50 first (multiply by \(\dfrac{50}{30}\)). Then plot (Test 1, Test 2 out of 50) and draw the least-squares line through the middle of the points.

steps.explain: Test 2 is out of 30 but the graph axis is out of 50, so convert each Test 2 score: divide by 30, then multiply by 50 (yellow row).

questions.stem: The results of two tests of students were analysed and the data is shown in the table. Note: Test 1 was out of 50 and Test 2 was out of 30. There is a student missing from the dataset because he was absent from test 2. Using the equation of the line of best fit, predict the score for test 2 if his score in test 1 was 30.
questions.hint: Substitute \(x=30\) into the line of best fit (which is for Test 2 out of 50), then convert the answer back to a mark out of 30 by multiplying by \(\dfrac{30}{50}=\dfrac{3}{5}\).

steps.explain: The line of best fit (Test 2 marked out of 50) is \(y=0.826x+2.84\). Substitute \(x=30\) (the Test 1 score), green dashed lines on the graph.
